newsitem.title: USA: Upbeat Clinton to set agenda for G7 summit.
newsitem.headline: Upbeat Clinton to set agenda for G7 summit.

text.p: President Bill Clinton arrived in Denver on Thursday to lay down a hopeful agenda for a weekend summit of leading industrialized nations, but some critics predicted the meeting will produce few breakthroughs on a host of international problems.

"The risk is the summit will be a mile high and a foot deep .. There's not much in the way of initiatives," former State Department official Robert Hormats, a veteran organizer of past Group of Seven summits, said.
The president, riding high on a buoyant U.S. economy, was expected to set high hopes for the 23rd summit of the group in a speech later on Thursday.

U.S. officials say Clinton will try to shift the focus of the summit away from traditional economic issues and towards global challenges more understandable to Americans, like fighting the drug trade, terrorism, cementing global democracy and cleaning up the environment.

He will also press for expandng democracy in Bosnia, increasing aid to Africa and will voice his concern over Japan's large trading surplus. He will declare that it is time to concentrate on "some of the new challenges we face in the post-Cold War era."

In an interview with Japan's Fuji television, broadcast on Thursday, Clinton said he also wanted to discuss with the G7 leaders and Russia's President Boris Yeltsin -- attending as an almost full participant for the first time -- the July 1 takeover of Hong Kong by China.
Clinton said he hoped China would respect human rights when it takes over the former British colony. China is not a participant at the talks.

Yeltsin, who has attended five previous G7 summits and has taken part in their political discussions, will this year also participate in talks on selected economic issues. He will be excluded only from a one-hour session on financial matters. Speaking in Moscow shortly before his departure for the summit, Yeltsin said: "I very much hope that in Denver it will finally be decided to turn the G7 into the G8."
The meeting is officially entitled 'Summit of the Eight" and Denver has rolled out the red carpet for the visiting leaders.

City officials say the three-day summit will cost about $20 million with the federal government paying about $7 million, mostly for security measures including having troops at the ready for emergencies including a chemical weapons attack.

The Denver summit stands in sharp contrast to the first G7 summit Clinton attended in 1993 when he came under attack for massive U.S. budget deficits that the other leaders claimed were a threat to economic stability.

In what one analyst described as a "golden era for the U.S. economy", unemployment is at its lowest level in nearly 24 years, the government budget deficit is small and shrinking, and inflation is low and stable.
Clinton will underline his country's strength at a time when European nations are battling high unemployment and Japan is emerging from years of economic woes.

The one foreign policy issue accorded a separate session, on Saturday, is Bosnia. Washington has initiated a new drive to rebuild solid democratic institutions in the war-ravaged country before an international peace-keeping force is slated to leave in the middle of next year.
